chapters.title: Chapter 2: Reading Where India Is in the Cycle

lessons.title: Credit Growth, Capacity Utilisation, and the Yield Curve as Cycle Signals

body.text: Credit is the fuel of the cycle, capacity utilisation is the pressure gauge, and the yield curve is the price of the fuel. Watch all three and you will see most turns coming before GDP confirms them.

children.text: Lesson 2.1 built a broad dashboard of indicators. This lesson zooms in on the three signals that matter most for sector rotation in India, because they speak directly to the sectors that swing hardest: banks and NBFCs live on credit growth, capital goods and cement live on capacity utilisation, and every rate sensitive sector lives on the yield curve.
Signal 1: Bank Credit Growth

markDefs.definition: Bank lending to agriculture, industry, services, and individuals, excluding loans to government agencies for procuring food grains. It is the cleaner measure of credit to the real economy, because food credit swings with government procurement.

children.text: India's economy still runs largely on bank credit. The number to track is year-on-year growth in
non-food credit

, which the RBI publishes fortnightly, along with a monthly breakdown by sector. When companies and households borrow faster, spending and investment are about to rise. When lenders pull back, a slowdown is usually close behind.

stats.context: The credit boom behind the 2003 to 2008 capex cycle

stats.label: Bank credit growth, FY17

stats.label: Non-food credit growth, Mar 2024

body.text: Check for mergers before trusting a credit growth number. When HDFC Ltd, a housing finance company, merged into HDFC Bank on 1 July 2023, its entire loan book moved into the banking system overnight. Headline bank credit growth jumped even though no new borrowing had happened. For about a year, analysts quoted credit growth both including and excluding the merger.

children.text: Growth vs Impulse

markDefs.definition: The change in new lending (the credit flow) from one period to the next, expressed as a percentage of GDP. A negative impulse means new lending is shrinking compared to the previous period, which tends to drag on growth even if total credit is still rising.

children.text: Credit growth tells you how fast the stock of loans is rising. But what drives spending is the flow of new credit, and what drives changes in growth is whether that flow is speeding up or slowing down. That is the
credit impulse

body.caption: New credit = the increase in outstanding loans during the period

body.title: Calculate the Credit Impulse
body.prompt: Outstanding bank credit in an economy was ₹150 lakh crore in Year 1, ₹170 lakh crore in Year 2, and ₹186 lakh crore in Year 3. GDP in Year 3 is ₹400 lakh crore. What is the credit impulse in Year 3, as a percentage of GDP?
body.explanation: New credit was ₹20 lakh crore in Year 2 (170 minus 150) and ₹16 lakh crore in Year 3 (186 minus 170). The change in the flow is 16 minus 20, which is minus ₹4 lakh crore. Divided by GDP of ₹400 lakh crore, the impulse is minus 1.0%. Notice that credit still grew 9.4% in Year 3. A headline that says "credit growing at over 9%" would sound healthy, yet the shrinking flow of new lending is already a drag on growth.

children.text: What the Credit Mix Tells You

Where the credit goes matters as much as how fast it grows. Credit growth led by loans to industry and infrastructure usually signals a capex upcycle, which favours capital goods, cement, and metals. Credit growth led by unsecured personal loans and credit cards signals consumption, but it can also signal risk building up. In November 2023, the RBI raised risk weights on unsecured consumer credit for banks and NBFCs from 100% to 125%, and on credit card receivables of banks to 150%, specifically to cool that lending. When the regulator starts leaning against a segment of lending, the lenders most exposed to it usually lose market leadership.
Signal 2: Capacity Utilisation

markDefs.definition: Order Books, Inventories and Capacity Utilisation Survey. A quarterly RBI survey of manufacturing companies that tracks new orders, inventory levels, and the share of installed capacity being used, reported both unadjusted and seasonally adjusted.

children.text: Capacity utilisation measures how much of their installed production capacity manufacturers are actually using. In India, the benchmark source is the RBI's quarterly
OBICUS

survey. The logic for investors is simple. When factories run well below capacity, companies can grow output without building anything new. When they run close to full, they must invest in new plants, and that capex wave flows into orders for capital goods, steel, and cement.

stats.context: Upcycle pushes utilisation into the zone that triggers capex

stats.label: Q3 FY26 (Oct to Dec 2025)
stats.context: Up from 74.3% in the previous quarter

body.label: The capex trigger zone
body.context: Industry bodies such as the CII have cited this range as the level at which fresh private investment gets triggered. It is a rule of thumb, not a precise threshold, and it varies by industry.

body.caption: What capacity utilisation implies for the cycle and sectors

body.text: OBICUS is a slow signal. Results for a quarter are typically released four to five months after that quarter ends; the July to September 2025 results came out on 6 February 2026. It also covers only a sample of manufacturers, not services. Treat it as confirmation of the capex cycle, and use order books and capex announcements from listed companies as faster, if noisier, supplements.

children.text: Signal 3: The Yield Curve

markDefs.definition: The difference between a long-term interest rate and a short-term interest rate, usually the 10-year government bond yield minus a short-term Treasury bill yield or the policy rate. A wide positive spread means a steep curve; a negative spread means an inverted curve.

children.text: The yield curve plots the interest rates on government securities across maturities, from 91-day Treasury bills to 10-year and longer government bonds. Its slope, the
term spread

, is one of the best known cycle signals in the world. Short-term rates are anchored by the RBI's policy rate. Long-term rates reflect what investors expect for growth, inflation, and future policy over many years.

body.caption: Yields in percent; multiply by 100 to convert percentage points into basis points

body.title: Three yield curve shapes (illustrative, not real data)

body.caption: Reading the shape of the curve
headers: What it tends to mean for sectors

cells: The central bank has cut rates to fight a downturn, while long rates price in future recovery
Banks earn more on the gap between deposit and loan rates; rate sensitives such as real estate and autos tend to benefit
The central bank is hiking; short rates rise faster than long rates
Rate sensitives start losing momentum; margins of lenders funded short-term come under pressure
Short rates are high and markets expect growth and inflation to fall, pulling long rates below short rates

body.title: Measure India's Curve
body.prompt: Using the readings above, a 10-year G-sec yield of 7.01% and a 91-day T-bill yield of 5.26%, what is the term spread in basis points?
body.explanation: 7.01 minus 5.26 is 1.75 percentage points, which is 175 basis points. That is a clearly positive, fairly steep curve. But look at why: short rates are anchored by an RBI that cut to 5.25% in 2025 and has paused, while long yields have risen on higher crude prices and elevated US yields. A steep curve caused by global inflation fears is not the same signal as a steep curve caused by rate cuts in a recovery. Always ask what moved each end of the curve. These readings are a snapshot and will change.

body.text: The yield curve is famous for predicting recessions, and famous for false alarms. The US 2-year to 10-year curve inverted in July 2022 and stayed inverted until September 2024, one of its longest inversions on record, yet the US economy did not fall into recession during that period. India's curve is also shaped by forces that have little to do with the domestic cycle: RBI liquidity operations, the size of government borrowing, and global bond yields. Use the curve as one input, never as a stand-alone timing signal.

body.title: Go deeper: corporate bond spreads, the credit market's fear gauge

children.text: The yield curve compares government bonds with each other. A second signal compares companies with the government: the credit spread, which is the extra yield a corporate bond pays over a government security of similar maturity.
Narrow and stable spreads mean lenders are comfortable taking corporate risk. That usually coincides with expansion and easy credit.

Sharply widening spreads mean lenders are demanding more compensation for default risk. After the IL&FS defaults in September 2018, spreads for NBFC borrowing widened, and funding for weaker NBFCs dried up, well before the full slowdown showed up in GDP.
Spreads for lower-rated borrowers usually widen first and most, so compare AAA spreads with those on lower-rated paper to see whether stress is spreading.
For sector rotation, widening credit spreads are a warning for NBFCs, highly leveraged companies, and real estate developers, the borrowers most dependent on market funding.
Reading the Three Signals Together

None of these signals is reliable on its own. Credit growth can be flattered by mergers, capacity utilisation arrives months late, and the yield curve is distorted by global forces. Read together, they give a far sturdier picture.

cells: Flattening as the RBI starts hiking
Steepening as the RBI cuts aggressively
Contraction, with recovery signals starting to build

children.text: Practice

body.title: Growth vs Impulse
body.question: Year-on-year bank credit growth has slowed from 16% to 13% over the past year. What is most likely true?
options: Credit is now shrinking, so the economy must be in contraction
The flow of new lending is likely weakening, which can drag on growth even though credit is still expanding
Nothing has changed, because 13% is still strong growth
body.explanation: Credit is still growing at 13%, so it is not shrinking. But a sharp fall in the growth rate usually means the flow of new credit is growing more slowly or shrinking, producing a weak or negative credit impulse. That can slow spending and investment before headline credit growth looks alarming. Capacity utilisation may or may not be falling; credit growth alone does not tell you.

body.title: Name the Shape
body.textWithBlank: When short-term government yields rise above long-term government yields, the yield curve is said to be ___.
body.explanation: An inverted curve means investors accept lower yields to lock in money for longer, usually because they expect growth, inflation, and policy rates to fall in future. It has often preceded slowdowns, but it has also produced false alarms, as the US inversion from 2022 to 2024 showed.

body.title: Read the Three Signals
body.scenario: Imagine the latest data shows: non-food credit growth has risen from 11% to 16% over a year, led by loans to industry and infrastructure rather than personal loans. The last two OBICUS readings show seasonally adjusted capacity utilisation at 76% and 78%. The RBI has raised the repo rate twice, and the gap between the 10-year G-sec and 91-day T-bill yields has narrowed from 180 bps to 60 bps. Corporate bond spreads remain narrow.
body.prompt: Which phase of the cycle does this point to, which sectors does it favour, and what would you watch as a warning sign?
body.modelAnswer: This is an expansion, probably mid to late. Credit is accelerating and is industry-led, utilisation is in the 75% to 80% zone where fresh capex gets triggered, and the RBI is tightening, which is flattening the curve. It points to a capex-driven upcycle that tends to favour capital goods, cement, steel, and lenders with strong corporate books, while rate sensitive consumer sectors may start losing momentum as rates rise. Warning signs to watch: the curve moving from flat to inverted, credit spreads starting to widen, credit growth rolling over while utilisation plateaus, and new capacity announcements piling up across the same industries, which is how the 2003 to 2008 boom ended in surplus capacity. Any one of these would be a reason to reassess cyclical exposure, not an automatic sell signal.

body.label: RBI Database on Indian Economy (DBIE)
body.description: Official RBI data on sectoral bank credit, Treasury bill auction yields, and government securities, the raw material for all three signals in this lesson.

body.text: This lesson explains economic signals for educational purposes and is not investment advice. Market readings such as bond yields are snapshots from September 2026 and change daily. No single signal, or combination of signals, reliably predicts the cycle or sector performance.

points: Non-food bank credit growth is India's core cycle fuel gauge: about 30% a year in the 2003 to 2008 boom, a six-decade low of 5.08% in FY17, and 19.1% in July 2026
The credit impulse, the change in new lending as a share of GDP, can turn negative while headline credit growth still looks healthy
Adjust credit data for one-offs such as the July 2023 HDFC merger, and watch the mix: industry-led credit signals capex, unsecured consumer credit can signal building risk
Capacity utilisation above roughly 75% to 80% tends to trigger fresh capex, which lifts capital goods, cement, and steel; OBICUS data arrives four to five months late
A steep yield curve usually marks early recovery, a flattening curve mid to late expansion, and a flat or inverted curve rising slowdown risk
The curve gives false alarms and is distorted by liquidity, government borrowing, and global yields; always ask what moved each end
Read credit, capacity, and the curve together to judge the phase, rather than relying on any single signal
